passages.text:
He is the man who has changed the world more than anyone else in the past hundred years. Sir Tim Berners-Lee may be a mild-mannered academic who lives modestly in Boston, but as the inventor of the World Wide Web he is also a revolutionary. Along with Galileo, William Caxton and Sir Isaac Newton, he is a scientist who has altered the way people think as well as the way they live.
Since the Web went global 20 years ago, the way we shop, listen to music and communicate has been transformed. There are implications for politics, literature, economics - even terrorism - because an individual can now have the same access to information as the elite. Society will never be the same.
The computer scientist from Oxford, who built his own computer from a television screen and spare parts after he was banned from one of the university computers, is a cultural guru as much as a technological one.
"It is amazing how far we've come," he says. "But you're always wondering what's the next crazy idea, and working to make sure the Web stays one web and that the internet stays open. There isn't much time to sit back and reflect."
He invented the Web, he says, because he was frustrated that he couldn't find all the information he wanted in one place. It was an imaginary concept that he realised.

For economists in the corporate sector, forecasting is usually a key function, and to do the job they draw upon a wide range of statistical data. But economic forecasting is a long way from a precise science. Forecasters must, after all, start somewhere and their assumptions about how an economy works can vary widely.
'The differences in beliefs are enormous; so varied and conflicting that economics is jokingly said to be the only field in which two people can get a Nobel Prize for saying exactly the opposite thing,' says William Sherden, author of the highly-regarded The Fortune Sellers.
Sherden argues that the record of economic forecasting is rather poor, especially for volatile statistics such as interest rates-although they do better for some stable statistics, such as government spending, and about the same for statistics such as real GNP growth and inflation.

fixedResponses.essay:
It is often argued that hometown plays a crucial role in the upbringing of a person. However, this hypothesis is not entirely true, as there are famous celebrities who became successful in their lives despite being born into poor families. In this essay, I will discuss the current Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi. Even though he comes from a modest background, he was still able to achieve great feats in his life.

Modi comes from a small town in the state of Gujarat, and in his earlier days, he was deprived of education because his family was not financially well-off. Moreover, for most of his life, he earned his living by selling tea at railway stations in Gujarat.

However, despite facing these hurdles in his life, he remained consistent and worked really hard. Later, he joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (an organisation that promotes Hinduism). After finishing his training with the RSS, he was later elected as the Chief Minister of the state of Gujarat because of his exemplary hard work and political manifesto of making Gujarat the best state in India, which he later achieved.

After becoming a successful Chief Minister, in 2014, he became a candidate for Prime Minister of the country. As the people of the country had already seen his work as Chief Minister, they made him the Prime Minister of the country. To this day, he still remains in that position.

In conclusion, from what has been discussed above, it can be concluded that with the right mindset, determination, and hard work, nothing is impossible. The place where people are born plays a very small role in deciding a person's future.
